lines: Call one real function to sync a file fully, and a separate one to sync just its data.
Do they genuinely make the same real system call underneath, or two different ones?
answer: Two genuinely different real system calls.
The data-only version genuinely isn't just the full version, renamed.

lines: Run it for real, traced: the full sync made one specific real system call.
And the data-only sync made a real, genuinely different one in its place.
Sync a file's own handle, then separately sync its parent folder's own handle.
Does the file's own sync already cover the folder, or are these genuinely separate?
answer: They're genuinely two separate real calls, on two different handles.
The file's own sync says absolutely nothing about its folder entry.

lines: Run it for real, traced: the file's own sync was one real call.
And the folder's own sync was a second, genuinely separate real call.
steps.takeaway: A file's own fsync says nothing about its directory entry — that's a second, separate call.

lines: Replace a file's content two hundred real times, the careful way: a temporary copy, synced, then renamed in.
Meanwhile a separate thread reads that same file as fast as it possibly can. Does it ever catch one half-written?
answer: No — it only ever sees the old content, or the new content.

lines: Run it for real: across many tens of thousands of real reads, racing two hundred real replacements,
the reader never once observed a length that wasn't the old file's, or the new file's.
steps.takeaway: Write-temp, sync, rename, sync-the-folder: that whole sequence makes a replace genuinely atomic.

lines: A well-known database retried a failed sync, exactly as its own code had done for twenty years.
What actually went wrong?
answer: The retry succeeded without writing anything at all.
The page it needed to write had already been marked clean by the first failure.

lines: The real finding is specific: a failed sync marks the dirty page clean regardless, on every file system tested.
So the second call finds nothing left to write, succeeds immediately, and the database mistook that for a completed write.
So, pulling this together: a full sync versus a data-only one, a file's own sync versus its folder's, and a retried sync that quietly lied, are really the same question, asked three times.
What, exactly, did that one call actually promise you.
steps.takeaway: Every one of fsync's surprises comes from the same gap: what a call promises, and what it covers.

lines: So, pulling this topic together: a full sync and a data-only sync genuinely make two different real calls.
A file's own sync and its folder's own sync are genuinely two separate calls that a safe replace needs both of.
And a failed sync's own retry can report success while having written nothing at all — which is exactly why the real fix is to crash and recover, never to simply try again.
